sections.title: A mixing desk for evidence
paragraphs: Picture a sound engineer mixing a band. Each microphone has a fader that can make that source louder, quieter or effectively pull it in the opposite direction; a master control can shift the whole mix before any musician plays.

A neuron works in a similar way. Each {{input}} is a signal, each of the neuron’s {{weights}} is a fader and the {{bias}} is the baseline shift: the neuron multiplies every input by its weight, adds those results, then adds the bias.

The size and sign of a weight both matter. A large positive weight makes a larger input push the combined score upward, a negative weight makes it push downward and a weight near zero makes that input contribute little.
The bias is not attached to one input. It shifts every case by the same amount, so a positive bias makes a positive decision easier to reach while a negative bias demands stronger positive evidence.

Do not treat one impressive weight as a guaranteed outcome. The final {{prediction}} depends on the input values, all the other weighted signals, the bias and the rule that turns the combined score into an output.
bullets: {{weights}} control how strongly and in which direction individual signals count.
{{bias}} controls the starting tendency shared by every case.
The combined evidence, not one number alone, determines the decision.

check.prompt: A spam neuron gives links a large positive weight. Which claim is the trap?
check.answer: Any email containing a link must be classified as spam
choices: Any email containing a link must be classified as spam
More links push the score upward when other values stay fixed
A negative trusted-sender signal could pull the score downward
The bias can make the neuron require stronger evidence
check.explanation: A large positive weight says how the link input influences the score; it does not decide the class by itself. Other inputs and the {{bias}} can still keep the combined score below the decision boundary.

sections.title: Move the boundary deliberately
paragraphs: Suppose a support team labels responses as safe to send or needing review. A tiny {{model}} uses inputs such as factual-support score, policy-risk score and whether the answer includes an unsupported claim; those labels become the {{target}} values it learns to predict.

If unsupported claims should strongly trigger review, that input needs influence in the review direction. If strong factual support should make review less likely, its weight should point the other way; training discovers useful values by changing weights to reduce {{loss}}.

Now imagine every response is sent to review, including clearly safe ones. The individual weights may rank risky answers correctly, yet the bias can place the boundary too low, giving the model an over-cautious starting tendency.

Changing a weight and changing the bias solve different problems. Adjust a weight when one kind of evidence matters too much or too little; adjust the bias when decisions are broadly too eager or too reluctant across many combinations of evidence.

In AiEval, you might compare two prompts on the same labeled cases and {{rubric}}. The evaluator’s explicit rubric weights are not literally a neuron’s learned weights but the comparison teaches the same discipline: hold cases and criteria steady, change one decision rule and inspect which errors move.

reveals.prompt: Risky and safe answers are ordered correctly but almost all are sent to review. What pattern should you investigate?
reveals.reveal: Investigate the shared decision boundary, including the {{bias}}. A broad shift may fix the review rate without changing which evidence ranks answers as riskier.

reveals.prompt: Only answers with unsupported claims slip through. What kind of change is more targeted?
reveals.reveal: Increase the influence of the unsupported-claim input in the review direction. That changes how one signal counts instead of shifting every case equally.

reveals.prompt: A change helps the training examples. Is that enough evidence to ship it?
reveals.reveal: No. Re-check on a held-out {{testSet}} so the improvement is not merely {{memorization}} of examples used to learn or tune the decision.

check.prompt: A review classifier catches risky answers but it also sends nearly every clearly safe answer to review. The ranking of cases looks sensible. What is the best first adjustment to test?
check.answer: Shift the bias toward requiring more review evidence
choices: Shift the bias toward requiring more review evidence
Increase every risk weight by the same amount
Train and report results on the test set
Remove the safe labels from the dataset
check.explanation: The broad over-triggering pattern points to the shared baseline rather than one misweighted signal. Test a more conservative {{bias}}, then measure both missed risks and false alarms on held-out cases.

sections.title: Apply the trade-off to spam
paragraphs: Your team deploys a spam {{classifier}} with three inputs: suspicious-link count, urgent-language score and a trusted-sender flag. Links and urgent language have positive weights toward spam, the trusted-sender flag has a negative weight and the bias sets the starting score before those signals arrive.

On the {{testSet}}, the classifier catches most spam but blocks too many legitimate password-reset emails. Those messages contain links and urgent wording, so increasing either positive weight would worsen the false alarms; blindly lowering every weight could instead let obvious phishing through.

Use the earlier distinction to make a controlled decision. If false alarms occur across many kinds of legitimate mail, lower the baseline tendency toward spam by shifting the bias; if they cluster around urgent wording, reduce that input’s weight and keep the strong link evidence intact.

Then compare errors, not just one average score. Count legitimate mail blocked and spam missed, choose the trade-off that matches the product’s risk and verify the change on held-out labels rather than tuning repeatedly against the final test cases.

The Bias and weights lab lets you move one neuron’s boundary by hand. Next, Activation functions explain the squash after the score (sigmoid, ReLU, tanh). The Neural network lab then shows how many neurons and weights learn together.
These are teaching simplifications: a production spam system needs richer data, carefully chosen thresholds and ongoing checks for new attack patterns.
bullets: Broad error across many inputs: test a change to the {{bias}}.
Error tied to one signal: test that signal’s weight.
After either change: compare false alarms and missed spam on held-out labels.

check.prompt: False spam alarms cluster around urgent wording, while suspicious links remain reliable evidence. Summarize the most targeted decision in a short phrase.
check.explanation: The failure is tied to one input, so changing that input’s weight is more targeted than shifting every case with the {{bias}}. Re-test afterward because reducing false alarms can also increase missed spam.

aside.title: Try the same decision in AiEval
aside.body: Compare two risk-classification {{prompt}} variants on the same cases and {{rubric}}. Inspect which variant reduces false alarms without hiding dangerous misses.

recapQuestions.answer: Weights scale individual inputs; bias shifts every case
choices: Weights scale individual inputs; bias shifts every case
Weights store labels; bias creates the test set
Weights choose the loss; bias controls the learning rate
Weights affect every case equally; bias scales one input
recapQuestions.explanation: Each weight controls the size and direction of one input’s contribution. The {{bias}} adds the same baseline shift after those weighted inputs are combined.

recapQuestions.prompt: In a short phrase, what should follow any weight or bias change?
recapQuestions.explanation: A plausible adjustment can still trade one error for another or fit the examples used to tune it. Held-out data gives a more honest estimate of how the revised {{model}} will behave on new cases.
